claims.text: Dynamic mechanical behavior in solidified equiatomic FeNiCrMn is controlled by a strain-rate- and temperature-dependent clustering-to-ordering transition within shear bands.
The clustering-to-ordering transition modulates dislocation mobility.
The proposed transition preserves a favorable strength-ductility balance in FeNiCrMn.
Homogenized, solidified equiatomic FeNiCrMn has a primarily disordered BCC or FCC matrix after standard casting and homogenization.
The initial FeNiCrMn material has minimal pre-existing chemical short-range order.
The controlled study varies loading mode, strain rate, and temperature while holding processing history constant.
Strain localization in FeNiCrMn shear bands leads to atomic-scale clustering.
Atomic-scale clusters in FeNiCrMn can transform from a disordered state to a chemically ordered arrangement under compression.
High-strain-rate compression initially induces disordered atomic clustering and subsequently enables chemical ordering in FeNiCrMn.
Chemical ordering within shear bands reduces local lattice distortion.
The reduction in local lattice distortion retards dislocation motion.
Retarded dislocation motion increases strain hardening.
Tensile loading produces less shear localization than compressive loading and therefore does not foster the clustering-to-ordering transition.
Under compression, lower temperatures produce higher peak flow stresses.
Under compression, increasing strain rate produces higher peak flow stresses.
The clustering-to-ordering transition is associated with an increased strain-hardening rate.
Tensile loading produces a lower stress response than compressive loading because it does not undergo the transition.
Quasi-static room-temperature deformation involves minimal shear localization, retains a predominantly disordered state, and produces lower peak stress and less strain hardening.
Extrinsic defects, secondary phases, contamination, or phase separation may obscure the proposed transition and alter the dynamic response.
Failure to detect compression-specific changes in clustering or ordering across the tested conditions would falsify the proposed mechanism.
